vignette:
Amir was twenty-three when it happened, three years ago now, walking home from the veterinary clinic where they worked as an associate. It was early evening in late September, that particular quality of dusk where the light drains fast and the streets empty quickly. They had been turning onto their street in a neighbourhood they had lived in for two years, a place that felt safe enough, when two figures emerged from behind a parked car. One grabbed Amir from behind—an arm around the neck, sudden and absolute—while the other demanded the phone, the wallet, anything of value. The smell hit first: stale cigarette smoke mixed with something chemical and sour, a scent Amir would later struggle to name but could never forget. There was no resistance possible; Amir's body went rigid, compliant, offering up everything without a word. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds. No weapon was shown. No one was hurt. But something essential shifted in those ninety seconds, something that Amir has spent three years trying to convince themselves did not really happen, or was not that bad—a story they still half-believe on the good days.

Now twenty-six, Amir returned to work in the weeks after because staying home felt worse. But the clinic, which had always been a refuge, became a minefield of invisible triggers. A client's cologne—sharp, chemical—would arrive before the person did, and suddenly Amir was back on that street, the smell crowding out everything else. A dog's sudden lunge during an examination would send Amir's heart into a panic that took hours to settle. The sound of a car door slamming in the parking lot would make Amir flinch, their body tensing as though the threat were immediate and present. Most difficult were the moments between patients, when Amir would find themselves staring out the clinic window at the parking lot, scanning the figures moving past, watching for the particular posture or gait of someone who meant harm. Dr. Patel, the senior veterinarian, noticed the change. Amir had always been confident with animals, quick to make decisions, willing to speak up in team meetings. Now Amir moved through the clinic like a ghost, apologizing for minor mistakes, deferring to every suggestion, becoming almost invisible. When Dr. Patel asked if everything was okay, Amir's throat closed. The words would not come—there was too much, too tangled, and by the time they tried to explain, the thread had vanished and they were standing there mute and ashamed.

The avoidance crept in gradually. First it was avoiding the street where the mugging happened, then the entire neighbourhood after dark, then going out at all became something Amir had to steel themselves for. Their partner, Jordan, would suggest dinner out or a walk through the park on a Saturday afternoon, and Amir would feel a familiar tightness in their chest, a cascade of reasons why it was not safe, why staying in was better. Jordan tried to be patient, but patience eroded over months. By the second year, Jordan had stopped asking. Amir realized one evening that they had not left the apartment except for work in six weeks, and even work required an elaborate mental preparation—the same route, the same times, the same scanning of every shadow. At home, the vigilance was worse. Amir had come to believe that safety was an illusion, that the mugging proved you could never truly know what was coming. Even inside, locked doors and windows checked twice, Amir felt the need to position themselves in rooms where they could see the entrance, to listen for sounds in the hallway, to check behind them when moving through the apartment. Jordan had learned not to come up behind Amir without announcing themselves first; the startle response was too violent. When Jordan would reach out to touch Amir's shoulder in the kitchen, Amir's entire body would jolt, heart racing, breath catching—a reaction that left them both shaken and reinforced Amir's conviction that danger lurked in the smallest, most ordinary moments.

What frightened Amir most was the loss of themselves. They could remember being happy, being confident, being someone who trusted the world enough to move through it freely. That person felt like a character from someone else's life. The constant vigilance had become so normal that Amir could no longer distinguish between caution and paranoia, between reasonable wariness and the exhausting conviction that danger was always one moment away. Three months ago, Jordan gave Amir an ultimatum—not cruel, but clear: get help or they could not stay. Amir realized they had become someone Jordan could no longer reach, and more terrifyingly, someone Amir themselves no longer recognized. It was that recognition, finally, that brought Amir to the clinic—not the veterinary one, but this one, to sit across from a therapist and try, once again, to find the words for what happened and what it had stolen. At twenty-six, Amir still had time to reclaim something of the person they had been, but the longer they waited, the more that possibility seemed to slip away like the September light on that street three years ago.
